tier_reason: First-party README table produced by public code (bench/bench_asm.cpp with bench/bench_harness.hpp, kernels in include/vectis/kernels/asm_kernels.hpp) on a named CPU (Intel i5-6500T) and the avx2 tier flags, but neither the README nor the repo names the compiler or version used for the benchmark numbers (GCC 15/16 appear only for tests and reflection; CI covers g++-13..16 and clang++-18/19), so it falls short of A; the -ffast-math 6.9x row has no benchmark code at all.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Compiler and version for the README benchmark numbers are not stated (README names GCC 15 and GCC 16 only for the test suites and reflection; CI builds with g++-13 to g++-16 and clang++-18/19). Build per README: CMake Release (CMake default -O3 -DNDEBUG; the bench_simd.cpp comment says -O2) with -DVECTIS_ISA_TIER=avx2, i.e. -march=x86-64-v3 -mno-avx512f -mno-avx512bw -mno-avx512dq -mno-avx512vl. bench_asm times each single call with std::chrono::steady_clock, reports the min of 21 runs after 3 warmups, and derives cycles/element from rdtsc averaged over the whole 21-run batch.
corrections.claimed_speedup: README 'The assembly verdict' table, dot_f32 at n = 1024 floats, L1-resident, min of 21 runs: scalar 1491 ns (4.92 cycles/element, 1.00x), scalar-4acc 679 ns (1.73 cycles/element, 2.05x), intrinsics 107 ns (0.338 cycles/element, 13.93x), asm 107 ns (0.333 cycles/element, 13.93x); against the four-accumulator scalar loop the vector kernels are about 6.3x faster (derived from page data). The README also states that the naive loop compiled with -ffast-math reaches 6.9x, but no benchmark in the repo measures that row (README text only). saxpy at n = 1024: asm 100 ns versus intrinsics 132 ns (1.28x), a small-n effect that disappears at DRAM sizes where asm sometimes loses (0.92x). SoA table (bench_soa.cpp): SoA vectorised 1.61x (n=8) and 1.37x (n=16) over AoS scalar at 28 KiB, 1.41x/1.28x at 448 KiB, 0.95x-0.96x at 7 MiB, 0.95x/0.87x at 112 MiB.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 0 stars, 0 forks, 7 commits, all on 2026-09-20 and 2026-09-21
corrections.caveats: Brand-new single-author repository (first commit 2026-09-20, 0 stars). The 13.93x figure is for hand-written intrinsics and GAS assembly twins in include/vectis/kernels/asm_kernels.hpp and src/asm/avx2_kernels.S, not for the library's vec<T,N> engine (bench_simd.cpp measures that, but the README publishes no numbers from it). The baseline is a deliberately serial single-accumulator loop that GCC may not reassociate without -ffast-math; the README itself says most of the gain is summation order (scalar-4acc already 2.05x, -ffast-math 6.9x, leaving under 2.3x for width and FMA). The benchmark compiler is not stated; the -ffast-math row has no benchmark code. Each 100-1500 ns call is timed individually with steady_clock, so timer overhead is part of every row; cycles/element is a batch average over all 21 runs, not the min. Measured on a powersave-governed i5-6500T; the author calls the timings noisy. Only AVX2 is measured; AVX-512 is compiled but never benchmarked, and the latest commit fixed false AVX-512 claims. SoA layouts lose to AoS at L3 and DRAM sizes, and AoS-to-SoA conversion costs 2-4x a kernel pass at large sizes.

notes: Numbers on the README match the record; downgrade A to C because the benchmark compiler/version is never stated (only inferred from the test matrix) and the -ffast-math 6.9x row is README text with no harness. The headline speedup is for hand-written intrinsics/asm kernels against a single-accumulator scalar loop, and the README itself attributes most of it to reassociation, not the Vectis vector engine.

tier_reason: This repo is the artifact of a peer-reviewed paper (Keiser and Lemire, Software: Practice and Experience 51(5), 2021; abstract per search snippet: lookup beats UTF-8 validators used in many libraries and languages by more than 10x), with public benchmark code (benchmarks/benchmark.cpp) and checked-in results; the repo names no CPU model or compiler version for its runs, and the paper could not be opened (arxiv.org unreachable), so it stays at B rather than A.

corrections.baseline: scalar UTF-8 validators: shiftless DFA validators in Hoehrmann style ('dfa', 'fdfa', 'bdfa', 'dfa2-4' rows), Fuchsia's FIDL string validator ('fushia' rows, fidl_validate_string) and UTF8-CPP (utfcpp) 2.3.4 utf8::is_valid ('utf8lib' row, vendored in dependencies/utf8_v2_3_4)
corrections.compiler_and_flags: CMake Release (default build type) with -Wall -Wextra -march=native on GCC/Clang (/arch:AVX2 on MSVC); the Dockerfile (Ubuntu 20.10) installs g++, g++-9 and clang++-9, but no compiler version is tied to the published results
corrections.caveats: Tier B rests on the peer-reviewed paper cited in the README (Keiser and Lemire, Software: Practice and Experience 51(5), 2021), which could not be opened here (arxiv.org unreachable; abstract seen as a search snippet only); the repo itself names no CPU model or compiler version. The README example output uses older row names (lookup4, basic, range) than the current driver prints (lookup4avx, basicavx, rangeavx). results/rome.txt and results/skylake.txt are checked in without CPU models (about 3.4 GHz and 3.69 GHz). No LICENSE file exists in the repo (none in the sidebar), so it is reference only; the README says it is for research, not production. Zwegner's AVX validator beats lookup4 on twitter.json in the README run (41.029 vs 37.000 GB/s). The production form of this algorithm is simdutf, which is already catalogued.

notes: README and results/skylake.txt numbers match the record exactly (hongkong.html lookup4 20.934 vs dfa 0.581, fushia 2.612, utf8lib 2.570 GB/s; skylake lookup4avx 17.081 vs dfa 0.615, fushia 1.578, utf8lib 0.512). The 'utf8lib' baseline is the vendored UTF8-CPP 2.3.4, a recognizable incumbent. This is the research artifact behind simdutf's validator (already listed); the orchestrator may prefer to fold it into simdutf as a duplicate.

tier_reason: First-party README table ('Approx. speedup vs. best compiler output') with no benchmark code in the repo (only Linux/*.s, Windows/*.asm, fast-array-ops.h, LICENSE, README), no CPU, compiler, flags or array sizes; the numbers also predate a 2025-12-11 correctness fix to several kernels, which caps them at C regardless.

corrections.baseline: unspecified 'best compiler output' scalar loops (the README headline also says 'compiler or STL', but no std::find / std::min_element / std::max_element baseline code or compiler is identified)
corrections.caveats: First-party table with no CPU, compiler, flags, array sizes or timing method, and no benchmark driver in the repo: the Linux/ (GAS .s) and Windows/ (MASM .asm) folders hold only the hand-written x86 AVX2 assembly kernels, and fast-array-ops.h is just extern "C" declarations plus overloads, so the core is assembly, not C++. The 'best compiler output' baseline is not identified. The table dates from 2020-2021; the last commit (2025-12-11, 'bugfix FastFind64, FastIdx16') fixed correctness bugs: FastFind64's small-n path compared only 32 bits (dword cmp instead of qword), the 16-bit min/max-index kernels broadcast the index vector with vpbroadcastd instead of vpbroadcastw, and FastMinIdxU8 started from a 127 sentinel instead of 0xFF, so earlier builds could return wrong results. Min/max index does not guarantee which index is returned on ties, unlike std::min_element/std::max_element, which return the first. Float/double min/max rows (28x, 14x) likely benefit from NaN semantics a compiler must preserve without -ffast-math; NaN handling is not documented. Several rows are small (32-bit integer min/max 1.1x, 64-bit 1.3x). x86-64 AVX2 only.

notes: README numbers match the record. No benchmark code exists in the repo, and the table predates the 2025-12-11 fix of real correctness bugs (32-bit compare in FastFind64, wrong broadcast in 16-bit idx kernels, wrong U8 min-index sentinel), so tier C stands with those shortcomings; tie-breaking differs from std::min_element.
